findings.title: Stage-2 cap only applies in the else branch — the full 200-candidate stage-1 set reaches Claude whenever the vector query returns zero rows
findings.detail:
`shortlist` starts as the *entire* stage-1 result (line 167 / 348). The `.slice(0, STAGE2_LIMIT)` that caps it lives ONLY in the `else` branch (line 193, mirrored at 371). So when `ctx.vectorReady && ctx.candidates.length > STAGE2_LIMIT` is true but `ranked.length === 0`, the `if (ranked.length > 0)` guard at line 184 (363) is skipped and `shortlist` stays at up to STAGE1_LIMIT = 200 entries. Those 200 are then JSON-stringified into one Sonnet request at line 222-229 (393-404) — each carrying `embeddedText`, which `buildPreferenceText`/`buildListingText` cap at 6000 chars (src/server/ai/embed.ts:87, 117) — against `maxTokens: 2000` and a `rankOutput` schema that accepts at most 30 matches (line 62). Result: a ~600KB prompt, a near-certain truncated/invalid response, and roughly a 10x cost overrun per run.

This is not an edge case, it is the default path on the pgvector-enabled box. `ranked` is empty whenever the SUBJECT row is unembedded, because line 177 (357) requires `l.embedding is not null` on the cross-joined subject — one unembedded listing empties the whole result regardless of how many contacts are embedded. And nothing in the tree ever produces an embedding: grepping src/ and scripts/ finds no enqueue site for `EmbedListing` or `EmbedContactPreferences` (only the new worker handlers at src/server/jobs/worker.ts:48-55), `pendingEmbeddings` (src/server/ai/embed.ts:275) has zero callers, and the `pnpm ai:embed` script referenced by embed.ts:238 and drizzle/0010_embeddings.sql:61 does not exist in package.json.

Fix: cap unconditionally after the if/else — `shortlist = shortlist.slice(0, STAGE2_LIMIT)` — rather than only on the non-vector path.

findings.title: Partial embedding coverage silently discards eligible candidates while match_runs records a clean vector run
findings.detail:
The stage-2 query filters `cp.embedding is not null` (line 178 / 357). When `ranked.length > 0`, line 187-189 (366-368) REPLACES `shortlist` with `ctx.candidates.filter(c => byId.has(c.contactId))` — i.e. only the embedded rows. With 200 stage-1 survivors of which 3 happen to be embedded, 197 contacts who passed every hard filter are dropped, not for scoring badly but because nobody embedded them, and they never reach stage 3.

The run record then actively misreports this. `vectorStageRan` is set true at line 185 (364), so `recordRun`'s note (line 499-501) is null — the note is written only when the flag is false. match_runs ends up saying stage1=200, stage2=3, vector_stage_ran=true, note=null: a thin result set that looks like the data rather than a coverage gap. That inverts the stated requirement that the matcher degrade honestly instead of silently returning nothing, and it inverts the file's own docstring at line 32-34 ("a thinner result set explains itself months later instead of looking like a bug").

Two things are needed: backfill the shortlist with unembedded stage-1 survivors up to STAGE2_LIMIT rather than discarding them, and record the embedded/unembedded split on the run so a later reader can tell similarity-narrowing apart from missing vectors.

findings.title: Stage 1 never filters on listing_type and never consults rent_pw, so the price gate is a no-op for every rental on both sides
findings.detail:
`listingType` is selected at line 79 and `rentPw` at line 83; neither appears in the WHERE at line 128-148. `contactIntent.intentType` is selected at line 123 and only passed to the prompt (line 227). The reverse direction (line 319-333) has no listing_type predicate at all.

The price predicates then break down for rentals. Rent listings carry their number in `listings.rent_pw` with `search_price_min/max` typically null (src/db/schema/stock.ts:136-138), and renters carry theirs in `contact_preferences.rent_pw_min/rent_pw_max` (src/db/schema/contacts.ts:187-188) — neither column is read anywhere in this file. Because lines 135-136 and 322-323 treat null on either side as "unconstrained", the price gate short-circuits to true for every rental. A buyer with a $700k ceiling becomes a stage-1 candidate for every rental in the tenant, and a renter with rent_pw_max = 450 becomes a candidate for every $2m house — and stage 3 pays Sonnet to rank them.

The same omission covers `bathsMin` (selected line 281, never filtered), `parkingMin`, `landSizeMin`, and `listings.availableFrom`, despite the docstring at line 23 claiming stage 1 filters "price band, beds, suburb, availability". The index built for exactly this predicate — `listings_search_idx` on (tenant_id, listing_type, search_price_min), src/db/schema/stock.ts:181 — goes unused. This is the root of the "stage 1 has no effective cap" problem: the cheap filters that should be trimming the funnel before it reaches the model are not running.

findings.title: matchListingsForContact never checks doNotContact, so opted-out contacts still get match rows written
findings.detail:
`doNotContact` is selected at line 274 but the guard at line 292 only tests `c.tombstonedAt || c.mergedIntoId`. The mirror direction filters it correctly at line 132 (`eq(contacts.doNotContact, false)`), so the two directions disagree.

A contact who has asked not to be contacted therefore gets rows written into `matches` by this path, and those rows surface unqualified on both screens — `matchesForListing` (src/server/queries/stock.ts:182-185) and `matchesForContact` (src/server/queries/stock.ts:198-203) neither of which re-checks `do_not_contact` — and are the feedstock for campaign drafting. The send gate is a separate backstop, so this is not itself a rule-1/rule-2 breach, but it puts a person who opted out in front of an agent as a live suggestion, which is exactly the state the flag exists to prevent.

findings.title: The (listing, contact) upsert lets the two directions clobber each other, mixing two incomparable score scales into one column
findings.detail:
`matches_uq` is `(listing_id, contact_id)` (src/db/schema/engine.ts:57, drizzle/0000_open_sentinels.sql:632) with no direction discriminator, so `matchContactsForListing(L)` and `matchListingsForContact(C)` write to the SAME row for the pair (L,C). `onConflictDoUpdate` at line 463-472 overwrites `score`, `reason` and `aiGenerationId` unconditionally.

But the two runs answer different questions. The listing direction asks the model to rank one contact against 20 sibling CONTACTS for listing L; the contact direction asks it to rank listing L against 20 sibling LISTINGS for contact C. Those scores are not on the same scale, and both are read back with `orderBy(desc(matches.score))` on the listing screen, the contact screen and the cross-tenant view (src/server/queries/stock.ts:185, 203, 221). Those orderings are therefore over a mixture of two ranking problems, and the one-sentence reason a listing screen shows an agent can be a sentence written to answer the other question entirely — the exact failure the non-optional reason string exists to prevent. Whichever run happened to go last wins, and nothing on the row records which one that was.

Related: nothing ever deletes superseded matches. A re-run after preferences change writes the new ~20 rows and leaves every previously-written row in place, so `matchesForListing` accumulates matches the current stage-1 filters would now reject.

findings.title: sql.raw() string-concatenated IN lists, with only incidental protection against an empty list
findings.detail:
Three sites build IN lists by string concatenation instead of binding: line 179 `sql.raw(`('${ctx.candidates.map(c => c.contactId).join("','")}')`)`, the same shape at line 358 for listing ids, and line 329-331 `sql.raw(`properties.suburb_id in ('${subs.map(s => s.id).join("','")}')`)`.

I traced all three sources and none is currently injectable: `contacts.id`, `listings.id` and `suburbs.id` are all `uuid` primary keys (src/db/schema/contacts.ts, stock.ts, shared.ts:25), so the values are driver-formatted UUIDs and cannot carry a quote. The finding is the construction, not a live exploit.

What is actually load-bearing is that the empty-list guards are accidental. Lines 179 and 358 are protected only because the enclosing condition is `ctx.candidates.length > STAGE2_LIMIT` (line 170 / 351) — a cost heuristic, not an emptiness check. Any future change to that condition (dropping the count check, or making it `>= 0` to always run stage 2) emits `in ()`, which is a Postgres syntax error, not an empty result — the matcher would break rather than degrade. Line 330 is guarded by `subs.length` explicitly, which is the right pattern. Additionally the 200-element literal defeats prepared-statement plan caching on the hottest query in the feature. All three should bind: `= any(${ids}::uuid[])`, or drizzle's `inArray()`.

findings.title: match_runs miscounts: stage2Count reports a stage that did not run, and several exit paths record no run at all
findings.detail:
Four separate accounting defects in the funnel record that is supposed to make "why did this contact not match?" answerable:

(a) `stage2: shortlist.length` (line 249, 425) reports 200 in the bug-1 path, describing a stage-2 that produced nothing. Combined with `vectorStageRan: false`, the row reads stage1=200 / stage2=200 / vector_stage_ran=false, which is not a funnel.

(b) `recordRun` is skipped entirely on three exits: `no-api-key` (line 71-73 / 264-266), `gone` (line 155 / 340) and `not-live` (line 156-158). The `not-live` case is the worst — the status check at line 156 runs AFTER the transaction has already executed the full stage-1 scan and the pgvector probe, so real work happens and leaves no trace. Move `status in ('live','under_offer')` into the listing SELECT's WHERE at line 99 so the scan never starts.

(c) `writeMatches` (line 450) and `recordRun` (line 489) open two separate `withTenant` transactions, so a failure between them leaves matches in the table with no corresponding run.

(d) `stage3: valid.length` counts what the model returned and survived the shortlist filter (line 235 / 410), not what was written. Duplicate ids in `data.matches` are not deduped before the loop at line 451, so a model that repeats a contact inflates stage3Count above the number of distinct rows written.

findings.title: Stage-1 LIMIT 200 with no ORDER BY makes the candidate set nondeterministic between runs
findings.detail: Both stage-1 queries end in `.limit(STAGE1_LIMIT)` (line 150 and line 335) with no ORDER BY. Which 200 rows come back is whatever the planner emits, so two runs of the same listing over an unchanged table can score two different candidate sets. Because the writes are upserts that never retire superseded rows (see the upsert finding), the union of every run's arbitrary slice accumulates in `matches` — and an agent watching a listing sees the suggestion list change with no data having changed. Order by something stable and meaningful (recency of preference update, or price-band closeness) so the truncation is a defensible "top 200" rather than a coin flip.

findings.title: hasPgvector caches process-globally and permanently, so the flag the matcher's honesty depends on can be stale or wrong
findings.detail:
`pgvectorChecked` (line 34) is a module-level singleton with no database key and no TTL; once set at line 40 it is never re-read for the life of the process, and `resetPgvectorCache` (line 45) is documented as a test seam only.

Two consequences. It is not keyed to a connection, so any deploy where one worker process serves more than one database answers for whichever it probed first. And it never re-checks: after installing the extension on a live box — the explicitly planned migration path, per drizzle/0010_embeddings.sql:10-16 — every running worker keeps reporting absent until restarted, so `persist` (line 249) silently keeps taking the text-only branch and the corpus stays unembedded. Since this flag is the single input to whether stage 2 runs (engine.ts:103, 294) and to what match_runs.note claims (engine.ts:499), a stale value makes the matcher's degradation report wrong in exactly the situation the report exists for.

findings.title: Null-vs-empty asymmetry in the property-type filter between the two directions
findings.detail:
Line 139 tests `property_types is null or ${l.propertyType} = any(property_types)`. An empty array is not null and `x = any('{}')` is false, so a contact with `property_types = '{}'` is excluded from every listing match. The mirror direction at line 325-327 handles this correctly with `c.propertyTypes?.length ? ... : sql`true``, so the two directions disagree about what "no stated type" means.

Not currently reachable: preference rows are created with only tenantId/contactId (src/server/actions/contacts.ts:91-93) leaving the column NULL, `propertyTypes` is not in `PREFERENCE_FIELDS` (src/server/ai/proposals.ts:20-30) so the AI proposal path cannot write it, and every seed fixture supplies a non-empty array. It is latent rather than live — but it is the same class of silent-empty-funnel bug the comment at line 106-110 says B1 already caught once, and the fix is to make line 139 read `coalesce(array_length(property_types, 1), 0) = 0 or ...`.

findings.title: Email messages carry sender ID but no unsubscribe — the only production call site drops it
findings.detail:
`sendMessage` composes the footer with `withComplianceFooter(req.body, req.channel, req.agency, { keyword: "STOP" })`. For `channel === "email"` the SMS branch is skipped and the email branch (gate.ts:145-152) only emits an unsubscribe line under `if (unsubscribe.url)` (gate.ts:151) — a field this call site never passes. The email footer is therefore body + "—" + agency name (+ licence): sender identification with no unsubscribe facility at all, which is precisely what Spam Act §18 requires and §10-per-your-comment claims to guarantee. The comment at send.ts:43-44 ("Added here so no draft, however written, can omit it") is not true of the unsubscribe half.

This is invisible because the parameter is optional (`unsubscribe: { url?: string; keyword?: string }`, gate.ts:138) — nothing type-errors, nothing throws, and the only test that exercises the email footer (tests/outbound.test.ts:287) passes a URL by hand, so it proves the function *can* emit one, never that the send path *does*. Confirmed there is no unsubscribe infrastructure anywhere in the repo: `grep -ril unsubscribe src drizzle` returns no route, no token, no /u/ handler.

Mitigation today: `sendEmail` (send.ts:154-168) is a stub that refuses, so no unlawful email can leave yet. That is exactly why this needs fixing before B6 wires SES — B6 is a transport change and will not touch this line. Make the unsubscribe non-optional for marketing (require a discriminated union where email demands a `url` and SMS demands a `keyword`), so a caller that has no unsubscribe cannot compile rather than silently sending without one.

findings.title: STOP revokes only one of the duplicate contact rows holding that number
findings.detail:
`recordOptOut` resolves the sender with `select ... from contacts where phone_e164 = e164 ... limit(1)` (route.ts:173-177) — no ordering, no handling of multiple hits — and writes the revocation plus `do_not_contact` against that single row (route.ts:181-197).

Duplicate contacts sharing a phone number are not an edge case in this schema, they are a designed-for state. src/db/schema/contacts.ts:120-135 says the phone index is *deliberately* not unique because §4 sends ambiguous matches to a merge review queue and a duplicate "has to be able to EXIST while a human decides". So the normal situation for an enquirer who came in twice is two live rows on `+614...`.

Failure: Jane exists as row A (from a portal feed, consent granted) and row B (from a web form, consent granted), unmerged and sitting in the merge queue. She texts STOP. Postgres returns row A; A gets the revocation and `do_not_contact`. Row B keeps `status = granted` and `do_not_contact = false`. The next campaign draft targeting B passes `checkConsent` cleanly — the contact is not tombstoned, not merged, not DNC, and its latest sms consent row says granted — and the agency texts the same handset again after she asked it to stop.

The merged-identity union in gate.ts:81-85 does not save this: it walks `merged_into_id`, and the whole point of the duplicate is that nobody has merged it yet. Fix by revoking across every contact row matching the number (and its merged children), not `limit(1)` — an opt-out is about a handset, not a row id.

findings.title: An opt-out from an unknown number is dropped, then the contact is created seconds later without it
findings.detail:
`handleReply` awaits `recordOptOut` first (route.ts:95), which returns `false` and writes nothing when no contact matches the number (route.ts:178). It then calls `ingestReply` (route.ts:98), which calls `resolveByPhone` — and that *creates* a contact for exactly that number when none exists (route.ts:145-155), with `do_not_contact` defaulted false and no consent rows at all.

So the ordering is backwards: the one code path that reacts to an unknown number by materialising a contact runs *after* the code that would have marked it opted out. Net result of a STOP from a number not yet in the CRM: a brand-new contact record that carries no revocation, no DNC flag, and no consent history — the only trace is the word "stop" sitting in an interaction body that nothing reads.

This also fires for a contact who *is* in the CRM but whose number was stored unnormalised (`phone_raw` set, `phone_e164` null): the lookup at route.ts:176 misses, the opt-out is dropped, and resolveByPhone then inserts a duplicate — which is finding #2's setup.

Partial mitigation: with no consent rows the gate returns `never_given` and refuses, so the very next send is blocked. It stops being a mitigation the moment anything grants consent for that number — a portal import, a web form submission that resolves to it, an agent ticking consent on the screen — because the STOP left nothing behind for the gate to weigh. Resolve (or create) the contact first, then record the opt-out against it.

findings.title: DLR 302 dedupe tests for any historical revocation, so a re-consented contact is never re-revoked
findings.detail:
The suppression handler skips writing a revocation when *any* revoked row already exists for (contact, sms) — `select id from consents where contact_id = ? and channel = 'sms' and status = 'revoked' limit 1` (route.ts:237-247), then `if (!existing)` (route.ts:249). But `checkConsent` reads the *latest* row, not the existence of a revocation (gate.ts:100-119). Those are different questions, and the mismatch inverts the guard.

Failure: contact revokes in March (row 1), fills in a web form and is re-granted in June (row 2). The carrier still holds the number on its opt-out blacklist. A send is attempted; MessageMedia accepts it (202, send.ts:134) and suppresses it, returning DLR 302. This handler finds row 1, concludes "already revoked", and writes nothing — and because the `do_not_contact` update sits inside the same `if (!existing)` block (route.ts:261-264), that is skipped too. The latest consent row is still June's grant, so the gate returns `allowed` on the next attempt, and the one every week after that.

Each of those attempts is also recorded as reality: the item is marked `sent` with a `sent_at` (approvals.ts:211-222) and an outbound `interactions` row is written (approvals.ts:229-239) for a message the carrier threw away. So the CRM's evidence trail — the thing you would produce if a complaint arrived — asserts a series of delivered messages to someone the carrier knows unsubscribed. The dedupe should compare against the current state (latest row per channel), not `exists(revoked)`, and the DNC update should not be conditional on it.

findings.title: Merged-identity consent is latest-wins, not strictest-wins as the docstring guarantees
findings.detail:
gate.ts:33-35 states the invariant: "The strictest state across the merged identity wins — the union is deliberate". The implementation does something else: it selects every consent row across `identityIds` ordered by `occurredAt desc` (gate.ts:92-101) and takes `rows[0]` (gate.ts:103). That is latest-wins across the union, which is not the same rule and diverges whenever the revocation is the older of the two.

Failure: Jane unsubscribes in March against record A. In June a fresh enquiry creates record B with a consent tick. A human merges B into A. The union now holds March-revoked and June-granted; `rows[0]` is the June grant and the gate allows the send. Under the docstring's rule it would refuse.

That direction is the common one, not the exotic one — duplicates exist *because* a new enquiry arrived, so the duplicate's consent row is usually the newer one and the survivor's withdrawal is the older. The test at tests/outbound.test.ts:153-165 only covers the case where the revocation is later (`loser` revoked `new Date()`, `survivor` granted a day earlier), so latest-wins and strictest-wins agree there and the divergence is invisible.

The two readings have genuinely different legal consequences and this function is the one place where that has to be decided on purpose. Pick one and make the code and the comment agree — and if it stays latest-wins, the test needs the inverted-order case asserting the intended answer.

findings.title: Consent ordering has no tiebreaker and trusts a caller-supplied occurredAt as its only sort key
findings.detail:
`orderBy(desc(consents.occurredAt))` is a single sort key over an append-only table where `rows[0]` decides whether a message may lawfully be sent (gate.ts:101-103). Two rows with an equal `occurred_at` order arbitrarily — Postgres gives no stable ordering for ties — so a revocation and a grant stamped at the same instant resolve by whichever the planner returns first, and that answer can change between runs of the same query.

Equal timestamps are reachable: bulk/legacy imports commonly carry date-only precision (midnight), and `occurred_at` is caller-supplied at every write site — route.ts:92 takes it from the provider's `date_received` string, and the intake pipeline takes it from the adapter payload (src/server/intake/pipeline.ts:122, `occurredAt: n.occurredAt`), which for the email adapter traces back to a header on an inbound message. Nothing clamps it, so a value in the past or the far future is accepted as-is.

That makes the sole ordering key for the compliance decision a field an outside party can influence: a back-dated revocation sorts behind an existing grant and never takes effect, and a future-dated grant outranks every subsequent genuine withdrawal permanently (consents are immutable — drizzle/0001:46-55 — so there is no way to correct the row afterwards).

Fix: add a deterministic secondary sort (`desc(consents.createdAt)`, then id) so ties resolve the same way every time; prefer the stricter status when timestamps are identical; and clamp `occurred_at` to not exceed the row's `created_at` at the write sites so a supplied timestamp cannot manufacture priority.

findings.title: No row lock and the provider call inside the transaction: duplicate sends, a live TOCTOU window, and a send that can roll back its own evidence
findings.detail:
`approveAndSend` reads the item with a plain `select ... limit(1)` (approvals.ts:117-121), checks `status !== "pending"` (line 123), calls `checkConsent` on the same unlocked rows (line 144), and then performs the outbound HTTP call (line 193) — all inside the action's single transaction (src/server/actions/action.ts:100). Four consequences:

1. Duplicate send. Under READ COMMITTED two concurrent invocations (two tabs, a Server Action retry, a double POST) both see `pending` and both reach `sendMessage`. The second UPDATE simply blocks then overwrites. The client-side `disabled={send.pending}` guard (approval-actions.tsx:64) is per-component and is not a concurrency control. `select ... for update` on the item would make the status check authoritative.

2. The TOCTOU rule 2 exists to close is still open. Nothing locks the contact or the consents between line 144 and line 193, so a STOP webhook committing in that window is not seen. It is a small window, but the whole design premise is that this check happens "milliseconds before the send" — with no lock the guarantee is probabilistic rather than serialised.

3. A rollback after the send destroys the evidence, not the message. Anything that throws after line 193 — the `interactions` insert (line 229), the `audit` insert (line 241), a connection blip — rolls back the entire transaction. The SMS has already left MessageMedia. The row reverts to `pending`, no interaction, no audit, and the reviewer's natural response is to press approve again and send it twice. For a Spam Act defence the failure mode is exactly backwards: the message survives and the proof of consent-checked, human-approved dispatch does not.

4. `fetch` at send.ts:106 has no timeout or AbortSignal, and it runs while holding a pooled connection (max 10 in production, src/db/index.ts:25). A hung provider pins connections for as long as the OS keeps the socket alive.

The shape that fixes 1-3: lock the item, re-check consent, mark the row `sending` and commit; send outside the transaction; record the outcome in a second transaction.

findings.title: The alphanumeric-sender guard checks a local env var, not the sender the provider will actually use
findings.detail:
send.ts:60-77 makes the correct argument at length — an alphanumeric sender ID cannot receive replies, so "Reply STOP" is not a functional unsubscribe and a marketing SMS from one is unlawful. The guard that enforces it (send.ts:95-101) then tests `process.env.MESSAGEMEDIA_SOURCE_TYPE`, a string this application writes about itself, rather than the sender MessageMedia will put on the message.

Two ways past it, both of them the default configuration:

- Neither env var set. `sourceType` defaults to `"INTERNATIONAL"` (line 93), so the guard passes; `sourceNumber` is undefined, so line 118 omits `source_number` and `source_number_type` from the payload entirely. MessageMedia then applies the account's configured default sender — which, for an agency that set up a branded sender at the provider, is the alphanumeric ID this guard exists to reject. The message still ships with "Reply STOP to opt out" appended (gate.ts:143), to a sender that cannot hear it.
- Env says INTERNATIONAL but the number configured on the account is a shared pool number. Replies to a shared number are not reliably routed back to this account, so STOP may never reach the webhook — same outcome, quieter.

Make the guard positive rather than negative: require an explicitly configured dedicated virtual number for marketing SMS and refuse when `sourceNumber` is absent, instead of refusing only when a local string happens to spell ALPHANUMERIC.

findings.title: Webhook auth is a forgeable static secret, compared non-timing-safely, and reuses the outbound API password
findings.detail:
Three separate weaknesses in one check (`if (!expected || presented !== expected)`, route.ts:76-79):

1. Not timing-safe. `presented !== expected` short-circuits on the first differing byte. The repo already has the right pattern — src/server/intake/form-token.ts:74 uses `timingSafeEqual` with a length pre-check — so this is an inconsistency, not a missing capability. Compare over fixed-length digests.

2. The secret is `MESSAGEMEDIA_SECRET` (route.ts:75) — the same value used as the HTTP Basic *password* for outbound sending (send.ts:84, 103). The inbound webhook credential travels in a plaintext header on every provider callback, through whatever proxies and access logs sit in front of the app. Leaking it does not just let someone forge webhooks; it hands over the ability to send SMS billed to the agency. These must be different secrets.

3. A static bearer is materially weaker than the sibling route's proof. src/app/api/inbound/ses/route.ts:87-107 verifies an SNS signature *and* pins the topic ARN, with a comment explaining that signature-without-topic-check was caught in the B3 review. This endpoint accepts anything with the right header — no signature, no replay window, no nonce.

What forgery buys an attacker, given this route's write surface: mass-revoke consent and set `do_not_contact` across arbitrary numbers (route.ts:181-197) — permanently, since consents are immutable (drizzle/0001:46-55) and the flag needs a human to clear; create contacts for arbitrary numbers (route.ts:145-155); inject interactions attributed to any number, which then feed the rolling brief and the AI; and flip any `sent` item to `blocked` with a fabricated reason by guessing a `provider_message_id` (route.ts:227-234). It cannot forge an opt-IN, which is the right asymmetry — but denial-of-marketing and evidence tampering are both real.

findings.title: The opt-out keyword matcher is wrong in both directions — it misses real unsubscribes and fires on ordinary replies
findings.detail:
`isOptOut` (route.ts:35-41) normalises, checks set membership, then falls back to "first or last word of a message of at most three words".

Under-matching (a real unsubscribe that does not stop the next send): the `words.length <= 3` cap rejects the commonest natural phrasings — "please stop sending me these" (5), "can you stop texting me" (5), "take me off your list" (5), "stop sending me property alerts" (5). Each is treated as an ordinary reply, no revocation is written, the gate keeps returning granted, and the next campaign message goes out. The docstring at route.ts:26-29 says the Act "does not require the customer to spell it correctly" — it equally does not require them to be terse.

Over-matching (an ordinary reply that permanently kills the relationship): `"no"` is in the set (route.ts:32) and matches as first-or-last word within three words. An agent texts "Are you free for a 10am inspection Saturday?" and gets "no thanks" — or "no worries", or "cancel the inspection", or "remove the sign" (all ≤3 words with an opt-out word at an end). Every one of those writes a `revoked` consent row and sets `do_not_contact = true` (route.ts:181-197). The consent row is immutable by trigger, and `do_not_contact` is an unconditional hard stop in the gate (gate.ts:72-78), so a live client answering a question is silently removed from all outbound contact and nobody is notified.

The two directions need different treatment rather than one heuristic: match a strict standard keyword set on a message that is *only* that keyword (plus punctuation), and separately scan any length of message for unambiguous opt-out phrases ("stop", "unsubscribe", "opt out", "remove me", "take me off") as whole words. "no" on its own is not an unsubscribe and should not be in the set at all.

findings.title: consentAtDraft is fabricated at send time when the draft never recorded one
findings.detail:
`consentAtDraft: item.consentAtDraft ?? "granted"` writes a draft-time provenance value at send time, from a check that happened now, for a moment nobody observed.

The column's meaning is explicit — "Consent as it stood when the draft was written" (src/db/schema/engine.ts:171-178) — and it is the input to the screen's "changed since drafting" badge: `item.consentAtDraft !== null && item.consentAtDraft !== item.consentNow` (src/app/(app)/approvals/page.tsx:22-24). That comparison is deliberately written to treat null as "not recorded, therefore not a change". Coalescing to "granted" defeats it: the row now asserts consent existed at drafting, so a later revocation renders a confident "changed since drafting" badge derived from a value that was invented, and an audit reading the row cannot tell a recorded draft-time check from a backfilled one.

This is the reconstruction the non-negotiable rules out — provenance captured at submission or not at all, the same principle src/server/intake/pipeline.ts:108-111 states for consent rows. The honest write is to leave it null; the send-time truth already has its own columns (`consent_checked_at`, and the audit metadata at approvals.ts:246-252, which correctly freezes `decision.grantedAt` and `decision.wording`). If drafts should carry a draft-time reading, capture it when the draft is created.

findings.title: Inbound SMS discards the provider message id, defeating the pipeline's replay key on a retrying webhook
findings.detail:
The reply schema parses `reply_id` and `message_id` (route.ts:44-45) and then never uses either. `ingestReply` routes through the `manual` adapter (route.ts:111-122), which hardcodes `messageId: null` (src/server/intake/adapters/manual.ts:36) — correctly, for its own use case: "the human is standing on the contact's screen... no message id exists — two phone calls are two interactions, never a replay" (manual.ts:9-11). SMS is the opposite: it has a stable provider id, and the webhook that delivers it retries.

The pipeline is built around that key. src/server/intake/pipeline.ts:96-105 relies on the message-id unique index to collapse redeliveries ("two SNS deliveries in flight together") and falls back to `findByMessageId` on conflict. With `messageId: null` none of that engages, so every retry inserts another interaction: the contact's history shows the same text three times, and the rolling brief and any AI summarisation read the duplicates as repeated contact.

Retries are not hypothetical here — this route returns non-2xx on unauthenticated requests (route.ts:78), unrecognised payloads (route.ts:87), and any thrown error, and MessageMedia redelivers on non-2xx. Pass `r.message_id ?? r.reply_id` through as the replay key (which needs an adapter that accepts one — the manual adapter is the wrong vehicle for a channel that has ids).

findings.title: The opt-out write is unguarded and runs first, so a bad provider timestamp loses the STOP entirely
findings.detail:
`occurredAt` is built as `r.date_received ? new Date(r.date_received) : new Date()` (route.ts:92) with no validity check. An unparseable or non-ISO `date_received` yields an Invalid Date, which is then handed to the `consents` insert (route.ts:191) and rejected by the driver.

The error handling around that is exactly inverted relative to what matters. `ingestReply` — storing a copy of the text — is wrapped in `.catch` and degrades to a console line (route.ts:123-125). `recordOptOut` — the legally load-bearing write — is awaited bare at route.ts:95, ahead of the ingest. So a throw there aborts the whole request before the message is stored at all: no revocation, no interaction, a 500 to MessageMedia. The provider retries, the same malformed field produces the same failure, and after the retry budget the opt-out is gone with no trace anywhere in the system.

Same exposure for any transient failure on that path (a lock wait, a pool timeout): the reply that would at least have left "stop" visible in the contact's history is lost along with it.

Validate the timestamp (`Number.isNaN(d.getTime())` → fall back to `new Date()`, and clamp future values per the ordering finding), and restructure so the two writes fail independently — an opt-out that cannot be recorded should be retried and alarmed on, never silently swallowed *or* allowed to take the message down with it.

findings.title: The approvals screen's consent pill disagrees with the gate that will actually decide
findings.detail:
`currentFor` (ops.ts:100-112) computes the pill from the contact's own consent rows only. It ignores three of the four things `checkConsent` weighs: `do_not_contact` (gate.ts:72-78), `tombstoned_at` (gate.ts:58-64), and consent rows on merged-away duplicates (gate.ts:81-85, 100). It also collapses every non-sms kind to the email channel (`kind === "sms" ? "sms" : "email"`, ops.ts:106), so a `social` item that carries a contact id renders an email consent state for a message that has no recipient.

So the queue can show a green "consent granted" badge on a draft the gate will refuse the instant it is pressed — a do-not-contact contact, a tombstoned one, or someone who unsubscribed through a duplicate. The reviewer has no way to anticipate the refusal from the screen, which undercuts the point of showing live consent at all (the comment at ops.ts:88-91 argues the badge must be live or it is "decorative").

The fix is to have one function answer this question. Reuse `checkConsent`'s logic for the pill rather than a second, laxer implementation that will keep drifting from it.

findings.title: The contact→listings direction matches do-not-contact people; the reverse direction excludes them
findings.detail:
`matchListingsForContact` selects `doNotContact: contacts.doNotContact` (engine.ts:274) and then never reads it — the guard at engine.ts:292 checks only `tombstonedAt` and `mergedIntoId`. The mirror-image path filters it in SQL: `eq(contacts.doNotContact, false)` at engine.ts:132.

A selected-and-unused column reads as intent that got lost, and the asymmetry has real cost: a contact who has asked the agency to stop still accrues `matches` rows, still consumes a Sonnet ranking call per run (engine.ts:375), and still surfaces on screens as a person to send this listing to. The send gate does catch it at the end (gate.ts:72-78), so nothing unlawful ships — but staff are being pointed at a target the system already knows it may not contact, and the agency pays for the suggestion.

Add the `doNotContact` check to the guard at line 292 so both directions of the matcher agree on who is contactable.

findings.title: Stage-1 SQL uses untyped `$n IS NULL` params — listing→contacts matching fails on every run (42P08)
findings.detail:
Lines 135 and 136 interpolate `l.priceMin` / `l.priceMax` as bare drizzle params in an `IS NULL` test:

    sql`(${contactPreferences.priceMax} is null or ${l.priceMin} is null or ${contactPreferences.priceMax} >= ${l.priceMin})`

Drizzle emits a placeholder for each `${}`, and postgres.js sends numbers with an unspecified type OID, so Postgres has to infer the type. A parameter whose only unambiguous appearance is `$n IS NULL` cannot be inferred and the statement fails at PARSE time, before any row is touched. Verified against the project's own database:

    PREPARE a AS select 1 from contact_preferences cp
      where (cp.price_max is null or $1 is null or cp.price_max >= $2);
    ERROR:  could not determine data type of parameter $1

(Reusing the same placeholder in both positions does not help — also tested, same error. Adding `::int` does fix it — also tested.)

The reverse direction, `matchListingsForContact`, casts every such param (`${c.priceMax ?? null}::int is null`, lines 322–324), and line 137 in this same query casts too (`${l.beds ?? null}::int`). Only lines 135–136 were left uncast, which reads like the author hit this error once and fixed one direction.

Consequence: `MatchContacts` — the primary direction, the one wired to the worker at src/server/jobs/worker.ts:39 — throws for every listing, burns all 5 BullMQ attempts, and lands in the dead-letter set. Because the throw happens inside `withTenant` before line 246, `recordRun` never executes, so `match_runs` contains no row at all: the funnel table built to answer "why did this contact not match?" is silent for the failure mode that matters most. Fix: `${l.priceMin ?? null}::int` in both clauses, matching lines 322–324.

findings.title: Installing pgvector after 0010 has run leaves the extension present but the columns absent, and the runtime check cannot tell
findings.detail:
The DO block branches on `pg_available_extensions` and adds the `embedding vector(1024)` columns plus the HNSW indexes only on the true branch (lines 32–55). scripts/db-apply.sh records each file by sha256 in `drizzle.__drizzle_migrations` and skips anything already recorded (lines 24–27), so once 0010 has applied on a pgvector-less database it will never run again.

That is precisely the transition the migration's own header advertises (lines 10–16: dev machine can't install it, AWS target has it as a one-line install). Walk it through: 0010 applies locally, text-only branch, hash recorded. Someone later runs `CREATE EXTENSION vector` on that same database — or the schema is promoted to a box where an operator installs it. Now `hasPgvector()` (src/server/ai/embed.ts:37-38) queries `pg_extension`, finds it, and returns true — but the columns were never created, because 0010 is hash-skipped.

From that point every code path that trusts the check breaks against a column that does not exist: `persist()` at embed.ts:263 issues `update listings set embedding = ...`, and the stage-2 queries at engine.ts:173-181 and 354-360 select `cp.embedding` / `l.embedding`. All raise `column "embedding" does not exist` — the matcher does not degrade honestly, it hard-fails, which is the one outcome the non-negotiable rules out.

The runtime check is testing the wrong thing. `pg_extension` answers "is the extension installed"; what the code actually depends on is "do the columns exist", e.g. an `information_schema.columns` probe for `listings.embedding`. Either that, or 0010 needs a companion migration that adds the columns idempotently when the extension appears.

findings.title: pgvector check is cached for the life of the process with no invalidation outside tests
When pgvector exists but nothing is embedded, the shortlist is never truncated and all 200 stage-1 candidates go into the Claude prompt
findings.detail:
`shortlist` is initialised to the full candidate set at line 167. Truncation to `STAGE2_LIMIT` happens in exactly two places: inside `if (ranked.length > 0)` (line 187) and in the `else` branch (line 193). Neither runs when `ctx.vectorReady` is true, `candidates.length > STAGE2_LIMIT`, and the vector query returns zero rows.

That combination is the normal state whenever the extension is installed but the embeddings have not been generated — which, per the finding on job wiring, is currently always: nothing enqueues `EmbedListing` or `EmbedContactPreferences`, so `cp.embedding is not null and l.embedding is not null` (lines 177–178) matches nothing. It is also the state immediately after enabling pgvector, and any time VOYAGE_API_KEY is absent so `embedDocuments` was never called.

With 21–200 stage-1 survivors, all of them get JSON-serialised into the user message at lines 222–229 (name, summary, softRequirements, intentType each) instead of the intended 20. Two concrete failures: the per-run Sonnet cost rises roughly tenfold against the ledger in `ai_generations`, and `rankOutput` caps the array at 30 (line 62) while the prompt never states that cap — a model handed 200 candidates that returns 31+ fails zod, `runTask` throws `TaskOutputError` (src/server/ai/run-task.ts:46), and because that throw precedes `recordRun` at line 246 the run leaves no `match_runs` row at all. `maxTokens: 2000` also makes a truncated, unparseable response likely at that input size.

Same shape at lines 363–372 in the contact→listings direction. The fix is to slice unconditionally after the vector attempt rather than only inside the two success branches.

findings.title: The provider HTTP call runs inside the action's DB transaction, so a post-send failure rolls the draft back to pending after the message has left
findings.detail:
`defineAction` runs the whole handler inside `withTenant`, which is `db.transaction` (src/server/actions/action.ts:100, src/db/index.ts:46). `sendMessage` at line 193 performs the real MessageMedia POST from inside that open transaction, and the durable record of the send is written afterwards at lines 211–239.

Anything that fails between line 200 and commit rolls back the status update, the interaction, and the audit row — while the SMS has already been accepted by the carrier. The row reverts to `pending`, the operator sees the same draft still sitting in the approvals queue with no indication it went out, and presses "Approve and send" again. The second attempt delivers a second real message. It also writes a second `interactions` row, and because the retry gets a fresh `provider_message_id`, `interactions_replay_uq` on (tenant_id, channel, message_id) (src/db/schema/contacts.ts:314-316) cannot collapse them — the index built for exactly this is bypassed. When MessageMedia's response omits `message_id`, `providerMessageId` is null (send.ts:142), the partial index does not apply at all, and duplicates accumulate unconditionally.

Secondary, same root cause: a pooled connection is held across network I/O, and `sendMessage` calls `getSecret` twice (send.ts:83-84), each of which opens *another* `withTenant` transaction while the first is still held. With `max: 10` in production (src/db/index.ts:25), ten concurrent approvals each holding one connection and each waiting on a second is a pool deadlock.

The send needs to be outside the transaction, with the outcome recorded in a short second transaction keyed on something idempotent.

findings.title: `consentAtDraft: item.consentAtDraft ?? "granted"` fabricates draft-time consent provenance
findings.detail:
On the success path the send writes `consentAtDraft: item.consentAtDraft ?? "granted"`. When the drafting step never recorded a consent state, this back-fills the column with `granted` — a statement about what consent looked like at a moment nobody checked, written after the fact from the outcome of a *different* check made at a *different* time.

The schema comment at src/db/schema/engine.ts:174-177 is explicit that this column holds "consent as it stood when the draft was written" and that holding both timestamps is what makes "changed since drafting" visible. After this line, a row where draft-time consent was genuinely verified is indistinguishable from one where it was invented, so the badge on the approvals screen and any later audit read a value that was reconstructed rather than captured — the thing the Spam Act provenance rule specifically forbids.

The block branch is consistent about this, incidentally: it sets `consentCheckedAt` but leaves `consentAtDraft` null (lines 147–155). That asymmetry is what the modified assertion in tests/queries.test.ts:67-69 is now relying on to find the seeded row. Leave the column null when nothing was captured.

findings.title: Inbound replies discard the provider message id, bypassing the replay dedupe index built for this
findings.detail:
`reply` parses `reply_id` and `message_id` (lines 44–45) and `ingestReply` then throws both away — the object handed to `ingestThrough` at lines 112–121 has no id field. It routes through the `manual` adapter, which hardcodes `messageId: null` (src/server/intake/adapters/manual.ts:36) because its contract is a human typing up a phone call, where "no message id exists — two phone calls are two interactions, never a replay".

An SMS webhook is the opposite case. The pipeline's dedupe is gated on `if (n.messageId)` (src/server/intake/pipeline.ts:70), and `interactions_replay_uq` is partial on `message_id is not null` (src/db/schema/contacts.ts:314-316), so with a null id neither fires. MessageMedia delivers MO webhooks at-least-once; every redelivery of the same text becomes another `interactions` row on the contact's timeline, which then feeds the rolling brief and the summarise job as if the person had sent the message twice.

Worse for opt-outs: `recordOptOut` (line 181) has no dedupe of its own, so each redelivery of a STOP appends another `consents` revocation row to an append-only table. Note the delivery-receipt path *does* guard against exactly this at line 249 — the reply path does not. Pass `r.message_id ?? r.reply_id` through as `messageId`, which is what the index exists for.

findings.title: Carrier suppression dedupe tests for any historical revocation instead of the current consent state
findings.detail:
Before writing a revocation for a 302 suppression the handler looks for any existing `consents` row with status `revoked` on the sms channel (lines 237–247) and skips the write if one is found — "Do not stack duplicate revocations on every suppressed send."

But `consents` is append-only and the whole design of `checkConsent` is that the *latest* row wins (src/server/outbound/gate.ts:88-103, and the test at tests/outbound.test.ts:108-118 asserts exactly that). Sequence: contact revokes in January; re-subscribes via a web form in March, appending a `granted` row; the carrier's own blacklist still has them, so an April send comes back 302. The January row satisfies the `existing` check, so no new revocation is written and `doNotContact` is never set at line 262. The gate reads the March grant as current and keeps authorising sends that the carrier will keep suppressing — the CRM believes it may message someone the provider has confirmed it may not.

The check should compare against the latest row for the channel (order by `occurred_at desc limit 1`, status = revoked), not against the existence of any revocation ever.

findings.title: A 302 delivery receipt whose approval item cannot be found is dropped silently with a 200 response
findings.detail:
`if (!item) return;` — the handler then falls through to `NextResponse.json({ ok: true, suppressed })` at line 270. A carrier-confirmed opt-out for which the lookup at lines 213–218 returns nothing produces no log line, no non-2xx to trigger a MessageMedia retry, and no record anywhere.

The lookup misses for several ordinary reasons: `provider_message_id` was null because the send response omitted `message_id` (src/server/outbound/send.ts:142); the tenant scope is wrong (`systemTenantId()` at line 73 resolves to the oldest tenant row, so under RLS the item is invisible for any other tenant); or the DLR arrives before the sending transaction committed. In each case the most compliance-significant signal the provider ever sends — "this number has opted out" — is discarded, and the `suppressed: true` in the response body claims it was handled.

At minimum log and return a status that makes MessageMedia retry, so the receipt is not lost. This is the one webhook branch where silence is the expensive outcome.

findings.title: Re-embedding without pgvector desynchronises `embedded_text` from the stored vector, and the staleness is invisible to pendingEmbeddings
findings.detail:
The no-vector branch updates `embedded_text` and `embedding_model` but deliberately leaves `embedded_at` untouched (lines 252–254). For a row that has never been embedded that is correct and is what makes the backfill work.

For a row that *was* embedded and is being re-embedded while the vector stage happens to be unavailable — the cached-check scenario above, or a transient degrade — it silently breaks the pairing the module exists to maintain. The row ends up with the *new* text alongside the *old* vector, and because `embedded_at` is still non-null, `pendingEmbeddings` (line 296, `isNull(contactPreferences.embeddedAt)`) does not list it as pending, so no backfill ever repairs it.

That defeats the stated purpose of storing the text at all (lines 28–31: "stored alongside the vector so a human can read WHY two things were judged similar"). The explanation shown to a human no longer describes the vector that produced the match. Either null out `embedded_at` when writing text without a vector, or compare stored text against composed text when deciding what is pending.

findings.title: `vector_stage_ran` is recorded false when pgvector ran fine and simply had nothing to narrow
findings.detail:
The `else` at line 191 is taken whenever `candidates.length <= STAGE2_LIMIT`, including when pgvector is installed and every row is embedded — there were just twenty or fewer survivors. `vectorStageRan` stays false, and `recordRun` then writes the note at lines 500–501: "Vector stage did not run — pgvector unavailable or nothing embedded." Neither clause is true.

The column's whole justification is the comment in drizzle/0010_embeddings.sql:92 — "False when pgvector was absent, so a thin result set explains itself later" — and the module header at lines 32–34 repeats it. As written the flag conflates three states that call for three different responses: extension missing (install it), nothing embedded (run the backfill), and fewer candidates than the cap (nothing wrong at all). An operator reading `match_runs` months later to explain a thin result set is given a reason that is wrong more often than right.

Record the actual reason — `ctx.vectorReady` and the candidate count are both in scope at the call site.

findings.title: Nothing enqueues the four new jobs, and the `pnpm ai:embed` recovery path referenced by the migration does not exist
findings.detail:
`EmbedListing`, `EmbedContactPreferences`, `MatchContacts` and `MatchListings` have handlers and queue names, but a grep across src/ and scripts/ finds no `enqueue()` call for any of them — the only hits outside queues.ts/worker.ts are the seeded dead-letter fixtures in src/db/seed/fixtures/sample-data.ts:1670-1671. The existing enqueue sites (src/server/actions/contacts.ts:370, src/server/ai/handlers.ts:133, src/server/intake/pipeline.ts:56) only emit `RebuildContactIntent` and pipeline jobs. So no listing or preference record ever gets embedded, which is what puts the matcher permanently into the untruncated-shortlist path described above.

The documented manual escape hatch does not exist either. drizzle/0010_embeddings.sql:61 and src/server/ai/embed.ts:238 both name `pnpm ai:embed` as the backfill that makes the pgvector-absent branch recoverable; package.json has `ai:backfill` and no `ai:embed`. `pendingEmbeddings` (embed.ts:275), the function that command would drive, has no caller at all.

The migration's central design argument — that skipping the vector columns is safe *because* the text is recorded and the gap is a one-command backfill — depends on a command that was never written.

findings.title: Email path never supplies an unsubscribe URL, so `withComplianceFooter` emits sender ID with no unsubscribe
findings.detail:
`sendMessage` calls the footer builder with `{ keyword: "STOP" }` and no `url`, for both channels. In `withComplianceFooter` the keyword is only consulted on the SMS branch (gate.ts:142-143); the email branch appends the Unsubscribe line solely under `if (unsubscribe.url)` (gate.ts:151). With no url the email goes out with agency name and licence and no unsubscribe mechanism at all — sender identification present, functional unsubscribe absent, which is half of what §10 requires.

The function's own docblock (gate.ts:129-133) says it is composed here rather than left to a prompt precisely so a message cannot go out without it, and the SMS branch enforces that with `?? "STOP"`. The email branch has no equivalent floor.

The test at tests/outbound.test.ts:286-292 passes a url explicitly and so cannot catch this — no test exercises the argument shape that send.ts actually uses. `sendEmail` is stubbed until B6, so nothing ships today, but the footer contract is wrong now and B6 will wire a working transport to it. Make the email branch refuse, or fail loudly, when no unsubscribe url is available.

findings.title: The test's provider guard clears env vars, but sendSms reads credentials from the encrypted secrets table
findings.detail:
`beforeEach` deletes `process.env.MESSAGEMEDIA_KEY` and `MESSAGEMEDIA_SECRET` with the comment "Never a real provider in tests: MessageMedia credentials stay absent, so a send that got past the gate fails at the wire rather than texting anyone."

That is not where `sendSms` looks. It calls `getSecret(tenantId, "MESSAGEMEDIA_KEY")` (src/server/outbound/send.ts:83-84), and `getSecret` reads the encrypted `tenant_secrets` row first and only falls back to the environment when nothing is stored — "the stored value wins, because that is the one a person can change without a deploy" (src/server/secrets.ts:127-132). The tests run against the developer's real database (`process.env.DATABASE_URL`, line 36) as the real seeded tenant (`systemTenantId()`, line 37).

So on any machine where someone has entered MessageMedia credentials in Settings → Credentials to exercise the send path, `pnpm test` reaches a live provider. "does not mark a draft sent when the provider refuses it" (line 217) grants sms consent, approves, and expects a wire failure — instead it texts `+6141…`, and the assertion at line 228 that the row is still `pending` then fails, after the message has gone.

The guard has to operate on the same source the code reads: delete the `tenant_secrets` rows for those two names in `beforeEach`, or mock `@/server/secrets`.

verdicts.reason: Real, and the mechanism is exactly as described. Stage 1 (engine.ts:128-150, 319-334) applies no embedding predicate, so unembedded rows are legitimately eligible. Stage 2's SQL then restricts to embedded rows (`cp.embedding is not null` at engine.ts:177; `l.embedding is not null and cp.embedding is not null` at :357), and engine.ts:187-189 (mirror :366-368) REPLACES the shortlist with `ctx.candidates.filter(c => byId.has(c.contactId))`. Because the guard is `ranked.length > 0` (:184 / :363), a single embedded row is enough to collapse 200 hard-filter survivors to that one row. `STAGE2_LIMIT` is a cap, not a target, so the remaining 19 slots are left empty and 197 eligible contacts never reach stage 3 — dropped for missing vectors, not for scoring badly. The `else` branch at :193 / :371 keeps unembedded rows, so the two paths disagree about eligibility, which shows the exclusion is incidental rather than designed (there is no comment justifying it). The audit record then hides it: `vectorStageRan = true` at :185 / :364 forces `recordRun`'s note to null (:499-501), and match_runs has no coverage column (schema/engine.ts:270-280, drizzle/0010_embeddings.sql:89-95), so the row reads stage1=200, stage2=3, vector_stage_ran=true, note=null — indistinguishable from genuine similarity narrowing. That is the exact failure the file's own docstring (:32-34) and migration comment (0010:92) promise not to produce. Partial coverage is the normal state here, not a corner case: no enqueue site for EmbedListing/EmbedContactPreferences exists outside worker.ts/queues.ts, `pendingEmbeddings` has no callers, `ai:backfill` only handles interaction summaries, and embed.ts:178/:225 permanently skip rows whose composed text is under 20 chars — a contact with only a suburb ("Suburbs: Prospect." = 18 chars) is never embedded yet passes every hard filter since null preferences mean unconstrained. No test covers this path. Concrete scenario: pgvector live on AWS, backfill run last week, 200 contacts pass hard filters for a new listing, 3 embedded since the backfill; agent sees 3 matches, match_runs says the vector stage ran cleanly, and nothing anywhere records that 197 qualified buyers were never considered. Only quibble is a one-line off-by-one — cp.embedding is not null is line 177, not 178 — which does not affect the finding. Related flaw in the same block: when ranked.length === 0 the if never fires and shortlist is left uncapped at up to STAGE1_LIMIT (200) rows sent to Claude with maxTokens 2000, because the .slice(0, STAGE2_LIMIT) exists only in the else branch.
verdicts.fix: Backfill rather than replace, cap unconditionally, and record the split. In both directions (engine.ts:184-194 and :363-372), partition instead of filtering: build `embedded` from the ranked rows (with similarity) and `unembedded` from the remaining stage-1 survivors (similarity null, preserving stage-1 order for determinism), then `shortlist = [...embedded, ...unembedded].slice(0, STAGE2_LIMIT)`. Move that `.slice(0, STAGE2_LIMIT)` out of the `else` so it runs on every path — this also fixes the uncapped 200-candidate prompt when `ranked.length === 0`. Track `embeddedCount = embedded.length` and `backfilled = shortlist.length - embeddedCount` and thread both into `recordRun`. Then make the note reflect coverage rather than only the flag: add `stage2Embedded` / `stage2Backfilled` integer columns to match_runs (drizzle/0010_embeddings.sql:89-95 and src/db/schema/engine.ts:270-280 — the migration is still uncommitted, so amend it rather than adding 0011), and change recordRun's note expression (:499-501) so a partial run writes something like `Vector stage ran on ${embeddedCount}/${stage1} embedded candidates; ${backfilled} unembedded survivors backfilled into the shortlist.` instead of null. Keep the existing pgvector-absent note for `vectorStageRan === false`. Since stage 3 now sees `similarity: null` for backfilled candidates, confirm prompts/rank-matches.v1.md tells the model to treat a null similarity as "not scored" rather than "scored zero", otherwise the backfilled rows get ranked last for the wrong reason. Worth adding a test in tests/ that stubs the ranked query to return fewer rows than STAGE2_LIMIT and asserts both that the shortlist is topped up and that the run note is non-null.

verdicts.reason:
CONFIRMED at src/server/matching/engine.ts:167-194 (and the mirror at 348-372). `shortlist` is initialised to the entire stage-1 result (line 167, bounded only by `.limit(STAGE1_LIMIT)` = 200 at line 150). The vector branch at line 170 reassigns `shortlist` only inside `if (ranked.length > 0)` at line 184, and the sole `shortlist.slice(0, STAGE2_LIMIT)` lives in the `else` at line 193. When `ctx.vectorReady && ctx.candidates.length > STAGE2_LIMIT` is true but the vector query returns zero rows, both guards are skipped and up to 200 candidates reach Claude. Identical at 348/351/363/371.

Reachability is not an edge case — it is unconditional on any pgvector-enabled box:
